## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Candābhajātaka* (Ja 135) is a short birth story in the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. The narrative framework relates that the Buddha delivered this teaching while residing at Jetavana, occasioned by Elder Sāriputta's solution to a question posed at the gate of Saṁkassa [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. In the story of the past, during the reign of King Brahmadatta in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was an ascetic living in a forest hermitage [Fausböll 1877]. When dying, he responded to the inquiries of his disciples regarding his spiritual attainment with the brief phrase *candābhaṁ suriyābhaṁ* ("moonlight, sunlight") before being reborn in the Ābhassara brahma world [Fausböll 1877].
The canonical verse (numbered 131 in Fausböll's edition) declares that whoever wisely meditates on the light of the moon and the sun attains the Ābhassara realm through absorption free from applied thought (*avitakkena jhānena*) [Fausböll 1877]. In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), this practice is interpreted in terms of meditation using the white and yellow kasiṇas (*odātakasiṇa*, *pītakasiṇa*) to attain the second *jhāna* [Fausböll 1877]. In the identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the Bodhisatta reveals that his senior disciple was the past rebirth of Sāriputta, while he himself was the Mahābrahmā [Fausböll 1877].
